diagnosis: Decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B

examinerBank.question: This patient has splenomegaly and ascites. Walk me through why you favour cirrhotic portal hypertension here rather than schistosomiasis, which is also common in this province.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Both cause splenomegaly and portal hypertension, but the discriminator is synthetic liver function. Schistosomal (presinusoidal) portal hypertension classically spares hepatocyte function, so albumin, INR and bilirubin remain normal. This patient has albumin 22 g/L, INR 1.9 and bilirubin 78 µmol/L, all markedly deranged, plus a nodular irregular liver on ultrasound and known chronic HBsAg carriage — all pointing to true cirrhosis rather than periportal fibrosis from schistosomiasis. He also has no relevant river or dam water exposure history.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks for explicitly naming synthetic function (albumin/INR/bilirubin) as the discriminator and linking it to this patient's specific values; partial credit for a vague 'his liver tests are worse' answer.

examinerBank.question: You elicited asterixis and an abnormal star-drawing test. Explain the pathophysiology of hepatic encephalopathy and why you would not order an ammonia level to help you here.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Portosystemic shunting and loss of functioning hepatocyte mass bypass the urea cycle's normal detoxification of gut-derived ammonia and other neurotoxins, which cross the blood-brain barrier and impair astrocyte and neuronal function, producing the clinical spectrum from mild confusion to coma (West Haven grading). Ammonia level correlates poorly with clinical severity and is not required to diagnose or grade encephalopathy — the diagnosis is clinical, based on mental state and asterixis, and management should focus on finding and treating a precipitant rather than chasing a lab number.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants mechanism (ammonia/neurotoxins, portosystemic shunting) plus the explicit teaching point that ammonia is not diagnostically useful — this is flagged as a commonly probed point.

examinerBank.question: His ascitic tap shows 120 PMN/mm³ and SAAG of 14 g/L. Interpret both results and tell me what you would do differently if the PMN count had been 300/mm³.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: SAAG ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertensive ascites (cirrhosis or cardiac), consistent with his cirrhosis diagnosis; a SAAG <11 g/L would suggest TB peritonitis, malignancy, pancreatic or nephrotic causes. A PMN count of 120/mm³ is below the 250/mm³ threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, so empirical antibiotics are not indicated based on this tap alone, though a low ascitic protein still puts him at high future SBP risk requiring prophylaxis consideration. If the PMN count had been ≥250/mm³, I would diagnose SBP regardless of culture result and start empirical antibiotics (e.g., IV ceftriaxone) immediately, plus IV albumin if bilirubin or creatinine criteria for renal protection were met.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks require correct SAAG interpretation, correct PMN threshold application, and the point that culture-negative does not exclude SBP if PMN ≥250; also credit for albumin criteria.

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your overall approach to this patient's management, from admission to long-term follow-up.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Immediately: admit, search for and treat the encephalopathy precipitant, start lactulose titrated to soft stools, correct hyponatraemia cautiously, and give thromboprophylaxis despite the raised INR since coagulopathy is rebalanced not protective. Diagnose and grade severity with Child-Pugh (ABCDE: albumin, bilirubin, coagulation, distension, encephalopathy) and MELD-Na — here Child-Pugh C. Definitively, start tenofovir for active chronic HBV, notify the case, and refer for hepatology/transplant assessment given advanced disease. Supportively, start spironolactone for ascites with salt restriction, ensure adequate protein intake despite encephalopathy, and avoid nephrotoxins and sedatives. Long-term, arrange 6-monthly ultrasound plus AFP for HCC surveillance indefinitely, endoscopic variceal screening since he doesn't meet Baveno criteria to omit it, and ongoing reassessment of Child-Pugh/MELD for transplant timing.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Looking for structured immediate/definitive/supportive/follow-up organisation covering the specific teaching points (ABCDE mnemonic, thromboprophylaxis despite INR, HCC surveillance, Baveno criteria) rather than a generic 'treat the liver failure' answer.

examinerBank.question: His wife mentions he seemed fine mentally until this week, but you only asked him directly and he denied any problems. Why is collateral history so important here, and what precipitants would you specifically screen for?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Patients with hepatic encephalopathy frequently lack insight into their own cognitive change, so family or caregiver collateral history is often the only way to detect early or intermittent encephalopathy. I would screen for common precipitants: gastrointestinal bleeding (ask about melaena/haematemesis and check Hb/rectal exam), infection including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (hence the mandatory ascitic tap), constipation, dehydration or diuretic-induced electrolyte disturbance, and any new sedative or opioid use. Treating the precipitant is often more important than escalating lactulose dose alone.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks for naming at least three precipitants (bleed, infection, constipation, dehydration/electrolytes, sedatives) and explicitly justifying the collateral history rationale.

framework: chronic liver disease presentation → compensated vs decompensated → aetiology screen → discriminate cirrhotic vs non-cirrhotic portal hypertension → mandatory ascitic tap → severity grading (Child-Pugh/MELD) → complication screen (varices, HCC, renal, encephalopathy) → management by decompensation status and cause

patient.name: Sipho Mkhize
patient.personality: stoic, downplays symptoms, embarrassed about the abdominal swelling and slow to mention confusion episodes his wife noticed
patient.openingLine: Doctor, my stomach has been swelling up and my wife says I'm not myself lately...

presentingComplaint: 3-week history of progressive abdominal distension and leg swelling, with recent episodes of confusion

history.fact: Abdominal swelling began gradually about 3 weeks ago and has progressively worsened
Abdomen now feels tight and uncomfortable, clothes no longer fit around the waist
Both ankles and lower legs have become swollen over the past 2 weeks, worse by evening
Wife reports he has been muddled and forgetful for the past 4-5 days, sleeping during the day and awake at night, and once could not find his way to the toilet at home
Wife noticed his eyes turned yellow around 2 weeks ago; he has also noticed dark urine
No vomiting blood or black stools, but has noticed easy bruising on his arms over the past month
Has felt mildly feverish and generally unwell for the past week; no rigors
Mild generalised abdominal discomfort but no severe localised pain
Was told he was a hepatitis B carrier around 15 years ago during a blood donation screen but never followed up or took treatment
Drinks alcohol socially, about 2-3 beers on weekends, denies heavy or daily drinking
Tested HIV negative two years ago at a workplace wellness screening
Mother died of 'liver problems' in her 50s; unsure if she had hepatitis B or cirrhosis
Has lived in Durban his whole life working in security; no history of swimming or bathing in rural rivers or dams
No exertional breathlessness, no orthopnoea, no known heart or valve problems, no prior TB
No diabetes, no hypertension, no previous hospital admissions, no previous surgery
Takes no regular chronic medication, occasionally uses traditional muti from a local healer for 'cleansing'
No known drug allergies
Married with 3 children, works night shifts as a security guard in Pinetown, non-smoker
Appetite has been poor for the past 2-3 weeks with mild unintentional weight loss, though hard to tell with the swelling
Bowel habit normal, no diarrhoea, no constipation, opens bowels daily

examination.general: Jaundiced, chronically ill-looking man lying semi-reclined. Mildly disoriented to time but oriented to place and person. Fetor hepaticus present. Bilateral asterixis demonstrated when arms extended and wrists dorsiflexed and held for 30 seconds. Multiple spider naevi over chest and upper arms (>5, blanch on central pressure, refill centre-outward). Palmar erythema. Gynaecomastia noted. No Dupuytren's contracture, no parotid enlargement.
examination.respiratory: Reduced air entry and dullness to percussion at the right lung base consistent with a small hepatic hydrothorax; otherwise clear.
examination.cardio: JVP not elevated. Normal heart sounds, no murmurs, no pericardial knock. No peripheral cyanosis.
examination.abdo: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a positive fluid thrill. Liver span reduced, edge not palpable (shrunken cirrhotic liver). Spleen tip palpable 3 cm below costal margin. Caput medusae visible around umbilicus. Mild diffuse tenderness on palpation, no rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds present.
examination.neuro: West Haven Grade II hepatic encephalopathy — disoriented to time, lethargic but rousable, asterixis present. Constructional apraxia demonstrated on star-drawing test. No focal neurological deficit. Pitting oedema to mid-shin bilaterally.

investigations.name: HBeAg / anti-HBe / HBV DNA
investigations.result: HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, HBV DNA 45,000 IU/mL (active replication, HBeAg-negative chronic infection)

investigations.name: Diagnostic ascitic tap — cell count and SAAG
investigations.result: WBC 180/mm³ with 60% PMN (120 PMN/mm³, below SBP threshold), ascitic albumin 8 g/L, serum albumin 22 g/L → SAAG 14 g/L (≥11 g/L, portal hypertensive)

investigations.name: INR and serum albumin
investigations.result: INR 1.9, albumin 22 g/L (both markedly deranged — confirms impaired synthetic function, against schistosomiasis)

investigations.name: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler
investigations.result: Small, shrunken, coarse/nodular liver with irregular surface, caudate lobe hypertrophy, splenomegaly (14 cm), moderate ascites, patent but narrowed portal vein with reduced flow; no discrete focal liver lesion seen

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 10.2 g/dL, WCC 5.1, platelets 88 x10⁹/L (thrombocytopenia — earliest marker of portal hypertension)

investigations.name: Liver function tests
investigations.result: Bilirubin 78 µmol/L (mostly conjugated), ALT 62 U/L, AST 110 U/L (AST:ALT ~1.8), ALP 140 U/L, GGT 95 U/L — transaminases only mildly elevated despite advanced disease

investigations.name: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine
investigations.result: Na 128 mmol/L (hyponatraemia — prognostic marker), K 4.1 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 95 µmol/L

investigations.name: Ascitic fluid culture (blood culture bottles inoculated bedside)
Ascitic ADA and Xpert MTB/RIF
investigations.result: ADA 8 U/L (low), Xpert not detected — against TB peritonitis

investigations.name: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
investigations.result: 12 ng/mL (mildly elevated, non-diagnostic; needs surveillance imaging)

investigations.name: Ammonia level
investigations.result: Not routinely useful for diagnosis or grading of encephalopathy — not sent

differentials.dx: Decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B
for: known HBsAg-positive status for 15 years, untreated
stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia)
nodular shrunken liver with splenomegaly on US
ascites with SAAG ≥11 confirming portal hypertension
deranged INR and albumin confirming impaired synthetic function

against: positive HBsAg with active HBV DNA provides a clear alternative and more likely primary cause
no Dupuytren's contracture or parotid enlargement

differentials.dx: Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension due to schistosomiasis
against: no rural river or dam water exposure
markedly deranged INR and albumin (schistosomiasis classically spares synthetic function)
nodular irregular liver morphology on US, not the periportal fibrosis pattern of schistosomiasis
age and known HBV carriage make this a poor fit
SAAG ≥11 g/L (TB peritonitis is typically low SAAG <11 g/L)
ascitic ADA low and Xpert not detected
liver morphology and synthetic dysfunction point clearly to cirrhosis
no Kussmaul's sign or pericardial knock
no history of TB or exertional dyspnoea/orthopnoea
liver appearance is cirrhotic-nodular, not congested-smooth

pathophys.Ascites: Sinusoidal portal hypertension plus splanchnic arterial vasodilatation (nitric oxide-mediated) causes effective arterial underfilling, activating RAAS/sympathetic/ADH pathways and driving renal sodium and water retention (peripheral arterial vasodilatation hypothesis)
pathophys.Hepatic encephalopathy: Portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatocyte mass bypass ammonia detoxification via the urea cycle; ammonia and other gut-derived neurotoxins cross the blood-brain barrier and impair astrocyte and neuronal function; ammonia level correlates poorly with clinical grade
pathophys.Jaundice: Loss of functioning hepatocyte mass reduces conjugation and biliary excretion of bilirubin, causing predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
pathophys.Thrombocytopenia / easy bruising: Congestive splenomegaly from portal hypertension causes hypersplenism with platelet sequestration and destruction; coagulopathy from reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors compounds bleeding tendency, though anticoagulant factor synthesis is also reduced (rebalanced, not protective, haemostasis)
pathophys.Spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecoma: Impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogens leads to peripheral hyperoestrogenism, causing cutaneous vascular changes and feminisation
pathophys.Hyponatraemia: Non-osmotic ADH release driven by effective arterial underfilling causes free water retention in excess of sodium, diluting serum sodium and marking advanced, high-risk disease

staging: Child-Pugh Class C (Albumin 22 g/L=3, Bilirubin 78 µmol/L=2, INR 1.9=3, ascites moderate=2, encephalopathy grade II=2, total ~12 points); MELD-Na markedly elevated given bilirubin, INR, creatinine and sodium; West Haven Grade II hepatic encephalopathy

immediate: Admit and resuscitate; identify and treat encephalopathy precipitant (screen for infection, GI bleed, constipation, dehydration, sedative use)
Empirical lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools per day; consider rifaximin if not improving
Diagnostic paracentesis already performed — PMN count below SBP threshold but low ascitic protein means high future SBP risk; keep low threshold to repeat tap if clinical deterioration
Correct hyponatraemia cautiously with fluid restriction, avoid rapid correction
Thromboprophylaxis with prophylactic LMWH despite raised INR — coagulopathy is rebalanced, not protective, against clot
definitive: Start tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for chronic HBV given active viral replication and decompensated cirrhosis — antiviral therapy indicated regardless of HBV DNA level in decompensated disease
Refer for hepatology/transplant unit assessment given Child-Pugh C and rising MELD
Notify hepatitis B (notifiable condition) and screen household contacts/family for HBV, including vaccination of susceptible contacts
supportive: Spironolactone as first-line diuretic for ascites, add furosemide if inadequate response, with close monitoring of renal function and potassium
Salt restriction (avoid strict fluid restriction unless Na <125 mmol/L)
Adequate protein intake (do NOT restrict protein despite encephalopathy) and dietitian referral for nutritional support and sarcopenia
Avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and other nephrotoxins; avoid sedatives that can precipitate encephalopathy
Pruritus management if cholestatic symptoms develop
followUp: 6-monthly abdominal ultrasound plus AFP for HCC surveillance indefinitely (chronic HBV carrier)
Upper GI endoscopy for variceal screening — cannot be omitted by Baveno criteria given platelets 88 and stiffness 38 kPa, both outside safe cut-offs
Repeat Child-Pugh/MELD-Na reassessment at follow-up to track transplant listing urgency
HBV DNA monitoring on tenofovir to confirm virological response
Long-term abstinence counselling regarding alcohol and avoidance of hepatotoxic traditional muti

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the presentation as acute decompensation (ascites, confusion, jaundice) rather than purely chronic or incidental
stationChecklist.answer: 3-week progressive distension, 2-week jaundice, 4-5 day confusion — classic multi-system decompensation
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 1-2: distinguishing decompensated from compensated disease is the watershed clinical judgement

stationChecklist.item: Actively screens for all decompensating events: ascites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy, jaundice, including asking the family about confusion
stationChecklist.answer: Distension, leg swelling, jaundice, dark urine, bruising, and family-reported confusion and reversed sleep pattern all present; no haematemesis/melaena
stationChecklist.why: Patients often under-report encephalopathy themselves — family collateral history is essential

stationChecklist.item: Screens for aetiology: alcohol quantity/duration, known HBV/HCV/HIV status, family history of liver disease, muti/traditional remedy use
stationChecklist.answer: Known HBsAg-positive for 15 years untreated, modest social alcohol use, HIV negative, mother died of liver problems, uses traditional muti
stationChecklist.why: Aetiology drives both differential ranking and definitive treatment (antivirals vs abstinence)

stationChecklist.item: Asks discriminating questions for non-cirrhotic portal hypertension: rural river/dam exposure (schistosomiasis) and cardiac/pericardial symptoms (exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, prior TB)
stationChecklist.answer: No rural water exposure; no dyspnoea, orthopnoea or TB history
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 4: must actively exclude schistosomiasis and cardiac causes before labelling as cirrhosis

stationChecklist.item: Examines for stigmata of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren's, fetor hepaticus
stationChecklist.answer: Multiple spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, fetor hepaticus present; no Dupuytren's
stationChecklist.why: Physical stigmata support chronic liver disease over an acute or non-hepatic cause

stationChecklist.item: Performs and correctly demonstrates asterixis testing (arms extended, wrists dorsiflexed, held 30 seconds) and a constructional test (star-drawing or number connection)
stationChecklist.answer: Bilateral asterixis positive; abnormal star-drawing test consistent with Grade II encephalopathy
stationChecklist.why: Explicit bedside technique flagged for OSCE demonstration; grading determines urgency and precipitant search

stationChecklist.item: Checks JVP specifically to exclude a cardiac/pericardial cause of ascites and hepatomegaly
stationChecklist.answer: JVP not elevated, no Kussmaul's sign or pericardial knock
stationChecklist.why: Raised JVP with ascites should redirect workup toward cardiac/constrictive pericarditis, not cirrhosis — key discriminator

stationChecklist.item: Examines for signs of portal hypertension: splenomegaly, shifting dullness/fluid thrill, caput medusae
stationChecklist.answer: Splenomegaly 3 cm, positive shifting dullness and fluid thrill, visible caput medusae
stationChecklist.why: Confirms portal hypertension as the mechanism of ascites

stationChecklist.item: Presents a ranked differential distinguishing cirrhotic HBV disease from alcohol, schistosomiasis, TB peritonitis and cardiac causes with explicit reasoning
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning with correct use of synthetic function as discriminator is the core exam philosophy for this framework

stationChecklist.item: States that diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory in every patient admitted with ascites and sends cell count, SAAG/albumin, protein, culture (bedside blood culture bottle inoculation), ADA/Xpert
stationChecklist.answer: WBC 180 with 120 PMN/mm³ (below SBP threshold), SAAG 14 g/L, ADA low, Xpert not detected
stationChecklist.why: Explicitly stressed as mandatory in the framework; PMN ≥250 diagnoses SBP regardless of culture result

stationChecklist.item: Requests INR and albumin as true markers of synthetic function rather than relying on transaminases alone
stationChecklist.answer: INR 1.9, albumin 22 g/L — both markedly deranged, confirming cirrhosis and excluding schistosomiasis
stationChecklist.why: Framework emphasises transaminases are often near-normal in established cirrhosis; synthetic function is the key discriminator against schistosomiasis

stationChecklist.item: Sends HBV serology/DNA and requests abdominal ultrasound with Doppler ± AFP
stationChecklist.answer: HBsAg positive, HBV DNA 45,000 IU/mL; US shows nodular shrunken liver, splenomegaly, ascites; AFP mildly raised
stationChecklist.why: Confirms aetiology and screens for HCC, which chronic HBV carriers require from age ~20

stationChecklist.item: Calculates or references Child-Pugh (ABCDE mnemonic: Albumin, Bilirubin, Coagulation, Distension, Encephalopathy) and/or MELD-Na to grade severity
stationChecklist.answer: Child-Pugh Class C (~12 points); markedly elevated MELD-Na
stationChecklist.why: Severity grading determines transplant referral urgency and prognosis

stationChecklist.item: Outlines management addressing each decompensation: precipitant search and lactulose for encephalopathy, diuretics for ascites, thromboprophylaxis despite raised INR
stationChecklist.answer: Treat precipitant, lactulose/rifaximin, spironolactone ± furosemide, prophylactic LMWH despite INR 1.9
stationChecklist.why: Coagulopathy is rebalanced not protective — explicitly flagged as a commonly missed teaching point

stationChecklist.item: Starts tenofovir for active chronic HBV and arranges 6-monthly HCC surveillance with ultrasound ± AFP
stationChecklist.answer: Tenofovir initiated; ongoing 6-monthly US/AFP surveillance, endoscopy for varices since Baveno criteria not met (platelets <150, stiffness >20 kPa)
stationChecklist.why: Definitive treatment of the underlying cause plus lifelong HCC surveillance is essential in chronic HBV carriers, especially African men
